claim: Neural systems use homeostatic plasticity to maintain normal brain functions and to prevent abnormal activity.
source: Neural systems use homeostatic plasticity to maintain normal brain functions and to prevent abnormal activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about neural systems supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Homeostatic mechanisms that regulate circuit output have mainly been demonstrated during artificial and/or pathological perturbations.
source: Surprisingly, homeostatic mechanisms that regulate circuit output have mainly been demonstrated during artificial and/or pathological perturbations.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of research in the field as described in the manuscript.

claim: The respiratory motor circuit in bullfrogs normally remains inactive for several months during the winter.
source: To establish the extent to which a naturally inactive circuit engages mechanisms of homeostatic plasticity, we utilized the respiratory motor circuit in bullfrogs that normally remains inactive for several months during the winter.
evidence: This is a factual statement about bullfrog biology that serves as the basis for the experimental model.

claim: Inactive respiratory motoneurons exhibit up-scaling of AMPA-glutamate receptors.
source: We found that inactive respiratory motoneurons exhibit a classic form of homeostatic plasticity, up-scaling of AMPA-glutamate receptors.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Up-scaling increased the synaptic strength of respiratory motoneurons.
source: Up-scaling increased the synaptic strength of respiratory motoneurons and acted to boost motor amplitude from the respiratory network following months of inactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer in Figure 2.

claim: Up-scaling acted to boost motor amplitude from the respiratory network following months of inactivity.
source: Up-scaling increased the synaptic strength of respiratory motoneurons and acted to boost motor amplitude from the respiratory network following months of inactivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing reduced motor amplitude when AMPA receptors are blocked after winter inactivity.

claim: Synaptic scaling sustains strength of the respiratory motor output following months of inactivity.
source: Our results show that synaptic scaling sustains strength of the respiratory motor output following months of inactivity, thereby supporting a major neuroscience hypothesis in a normal context for an adult animal.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Homeostatic and compensatory plasticity maintains neuronal function through a suite of synaptic and intrinsic mechanisms.
source: Homeostatic and compensatory plasticity maintains neuronal function through a suite of synaptic and intrinsic mechanisms (Pozo and Goda, 2010; Schulz and Lane, 2017; Turrigiano, 2011), with the ultimate goal being preservation of normal network function.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: Synaptic scaling is a slow and global form of synaptic plasticity where excitatory synaptic strength increases or decreases equally across all synapses.
source: The most prominent mechanisms used to counter disturbances in neuronal activity include synaptic scaling, a slow and global form of synaptic plasticity where excitatory synaptic strength increases or decreases equally across all synapses (Turrigiano et al., 1998), modulation of presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Davis, 2013), and altering voltage-gated membrane conductances (e.g. Na+, K+, and Ca2+ channels) (Desai et al., 1999; Ransdell et al., 2012; Wilhelm et al., 2009).
evidence: This definition is supported by citation to foundational work by Turrigiano et al., 1998.

claim: Manipulations that perturb neuronal activity in vitro are the most common experimental approaches to evoke homeostatic plasticity.
source: Manipulations that perturb neuronal activity in vitro are, by far, the most common experimental approaches to evoke homeostatic plasticity (Williams et al., 2013), leaving many open questions as to what normal scenarios require homeostatic mechanisms to regulate circuit output and behavior.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Williams et al., 2013 and reflects the current state of the field.

claim: In developing rodents, neurons in the visual cortex undergo synaptic scaling at the onset of visual experience.
source: In developing rodents, neurons in the visual cortex undergo synaptic scaling at the onset of visual experience (Desai et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a specific example from the literature supported by citation to Desai et al., 2002.

claim: Neurons in the retinotectal circuit of Xenopus laevis homeostatically decrease their intrinsic excitability to compensate for developmental increases in excitatory synaptic inputs.
source: Also within the visual system, neurons in the retinotectal circuit of the aquatic frog, Xenopus laveis, homeostatically decrease their intrinsic excitability to compensate for developmental increases in excitatory synaptic inputs (Pratt and Aizenman, 2007).
evidence: This is a specific example from the literature supported by citation to Pratt and Aizenman, 2007.

claim: Plasticity in the dynamic regulation of synaptic strength compensates for variability in neuron number in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion.
source: Additionally, plasticity in the dynamic regulation of synaptic strength seems to compensate for variability in neuron number in the crustacean stomatogastric ganglion (Daur et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a specific example from the literature supported by citation to Daur et al., 2012.

claim: American bullfrogs often overwinter in ice-covered ponds with no need to use their lungs for breathing during cold winter months due to adequate skin gas exchange at low temperatures.
source: American bullfrogs often overwinter in ice-covered ponds with no need to use their lungs for breathing during cold winter months due to adequate skin gas exchange at low temperatures (Tattersall and Ultsch, 2008).
evidence: This statement about bullfrog biology is supported by citation to Tattersall and Ultsch, 2008.

claim: Frogs retain a relatively high locomotor capacity during overwintering submergence.
source: Although frogs retain a relatively high locomotor capacity during overwintering submergence (Tattersall and Boutilier, 1999), important muscles of the respiratory apparatus, buccal floor constrictors and glottal dilators, are inactive during cold-submergence (Santin and Hartzler, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Tattersall and Boutilier, 1999.

claim: Important muscles of the respiratory apparatus, buccal floor constrictors and glottal dilators, are inactive during cold-submergence.
source: Although frogs retain a relatively high locomotor capacity during overwintering submergence (Tattersall and Boutilier, 1999), important muscles of the respiratory apparatus, buccal floor constrictors and glottal dilators, are inactive during cold-submergence (Santin and Hartzler, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Santin and Hartzler, 2017.

claim: Upon forced emergence at warm temperature, bullfrogs immediately exhibit breathing movements after months of respiratory motor inactivity.
source: Despite months of respiratory motor inactivity, upon forced emergence at warm temperature bullfrogs immediately exhibit breathing movements, ventilate to match resting metabolic demands, increase ventilation during exposure to low oxygen, and generate respiratory motor output from the brainstem (Santin and Hartzler, 2016a; Santin and Hartzler, 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Santin and Hartzler, 2016a and 2016b.

claim: Bullfrogs ventilate to match resting metabolic demands after months of respiratory motor inactivity.
source: Despite months of respiratory motor inactivity, upon forced emergence at warm temperature bullfrogs immediately exhibit breathing movements, ventilate to match resting metabolic demands, increase ventilation during exposure to low oxygen, and generate respiratory motor output from the brainstem (Santin and Hartzler, 2016a; Santin and Hartzler, 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Santin and Hartzler, 2016a and 2016b.

claim: Bullfrogs increase ventilation during exposure to low oxygen after months of respiratory motor inactivity.
source: Despite months of respiratory motor inactivity, upon forced emergence at warm temperature bullfrogs immediately exhibit breathing movements, ventilate to match resting metabolic demands, increase ventilation during exposure to low oxygen, and generate respiratory motor output from the brainstem (Santin and Hartzler, 2016a; Santin and Hartzler, 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Santin and Hartzler, 2016a and 2016b.

claim: Bullfrogs generate respiratory motor output from the brainstem after months of respiratory motor inactivity.
source: Despite months of respiratory motor inactivity, upon forced emergence at warm temperature bullfrogs immediately exhibit breathing movements, ventilate to match resting metabolic demands, increase ventilation during exposure to low oxygen, and generate respiratory motor output from the brainstem (Santin and Hartzler, 2016a; Santin and Hartzler, 2016b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Santin and Hartzler, 2016a and 2016b.

claim: Increases in excitatory synaptic transmission occur during inactivity/AMPA-glutamate receptor blockade in vitro.
source: Increases in excitatory synaptic transmission occur during inactivity/AMPA-glutamate receptor blockade in vitro (Fong et al., 2015; Turrigiano et al., 1998) and in vivo (Hengen et al., 2013; Knogler et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fong et al., 2015 and Turrigiano et al., 1998.

claim: Increases in excitatory synaptic transmission occur during inactivity/AMPA-glutamate receptor blockade in vivo.
source: Increases in excitatory synaptic transmission occur during inactivity/AMPA-glutamate receptor blockade in vitro (Fong et al., 2015; Turrigiano et al., 1998) and in vivo (Hengen et al., 2013; Knogler et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Hengen et al., 2013 and Knogler et al., 2010.

claim: The amplitude and charge transfer of mEPSCs mediated by AMPA-glutamate receptors were increased in respiratory motoneurons after overwintering inactivity.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the amplitude and charge transfer of mEPSCs mediated by AMPA-glutamate receptors were increased in respiratory motoneurons after overwintering inactivity (Figure 2A–D).
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2A-D.

claim: mEPSC frequency did not change after overwintering inactivity.
source: In contrast, we did not observe changes in mEPSC frequency (Figure 2E), suggesting a similar number of glutamate release sites onto respiratory motoneurons in brainstem slices.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: A similar number of glutamate release sites exist onto respiratory motoneurons in brainstem slices after overwintering inactivity.
source: In contrast, we did not observe changes in mEPSC frequency (Figure 2E), suggesting a similar number of glutamate release sites onto respiratory motoneurons in brainstem slices.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of change in mEPSC frequency shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Charge transfer (mEPSC area) is more robust against space clamp errors than mEPSC amplitude.
source: Although the mEPSC amplitude is prone to dendritic filtering, charge transfer (i.e. mEPSC area) is more robust against space clamp errors (Spruston et al., 1993).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Spruston et al., 1993.

claim: Increases in both amplitude and charge transfer of the mEPSC suggest an enhancement of post-synaptic AMPA receptor function rather than changes in dendritic filtering properties of motoneurons.
source: Thus, increases in both amplitude and charge transfer of the mEPSC suggest an enhancement of post-synaptic AMPA receptor function rather than changes in dendritic filtering properties of motoneurons (Han and Stevens, 2009).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citation to Han and Stevens, 2009 and the experimental data.

claim: Neuronal input resistance did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons.
source: Consistent with this assertion, parameters influencing and influenced by dendritic filtering, neuronal input resistance and mEPSC rise time, respectively, did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: mEPSC rise time did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons.
source: Consistent with this assertion, parameters influencing and influenced by dendritic filtering, neuronal input resistance and mEPSC rise time, respectively, did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons (Figure 2F–G).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Respiratory motoneurons have enhanced excitatory synaptic strength after winter inactivity.
source: These results indicate that respiratory motoneurons have enhanced excitatory synaptic strength after winter inactivity presumably by up-regulating postsynaptic function of AMPA-glutamate receptors.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental data showing increased mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer.

claim: Increased excitatory synaptic strength of neurons responding to reductions in activity typically follows a multiplicative scaling relationship in dissociated culture.
source: Increased excitatory synaptic strength of neurons responding to reductions in activity typically follows a multiplicative scaling relationship in dissociated culture (Fong et al., 2015; Turrigiano et al., 1998) and in vivo (Knogler et al., 2010; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013), implying that all measurable synapses increase in strength relatively by the same extent.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fong et al., 2015 and Turrigiano et al., 1998.

claim: Increased excitatory synaptic strength of neurons responding to reductions in activity typically follows a multiplicative scaling relationship in vivo.
source: Increased excitatory synaptic strength of neurons responding to reductions in activity typically follows a multiplicative scaling relationship in dissociated culture (Fong et al., 2015; Turrigiano et al., 1998) and in vivo (Knogler et al., 2010; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013), implying that all measurable synapses increase in strength relatively by the same extent.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Knogler et al., 2010 and Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013.

claim: Synaptic scaling maintains relative synaptic strength in the face of disturbances in neuronal activity.
source: Thus, synaptic scaling maintains relative synaptic strength in the face of disturbances in neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a general principle of synaptic scaling supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: A rank order plot following long-term potentiation (LTP) is better approximated by an exponential curve.
source: In contrast to synaptic scaling, a rank order plot following long-term potentiation (LTP) - a rapid and synapse-specific form of synaptic plasticity- is better approximated by an exponential curve (Gainey et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Gainey et al., 2009.

claim: The rank order plot of mEPSC amplitudes from control and winter inactivity vagal respiratory motoneurons is well-fit by a linear regression (r2 = 0.99).
source: When rank ordering an equal number of mEPSC amplitudes from control and winter inactivity vagal respiratory motoneurons (black dots; 50 mEPSCs from 16 neurons in each group), the plot is well-fit by a linear regression (r2 = 0.99; Figure 3A; dashed blue line), rather than an exponential curve (r2 = 0.73; Figure 3A; dashed black line).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The rank order plot of mEPSC amplitudes from control and winter inactivity vagal respiratory motoneurons is not well-fit by an exponential curve (r2 = 0.73).
source: When rank ordering an equal number of mEPSC amplitudes from control and winter inactivity vagal respiratory motoneurons (black dots; 50 mEPSCs from 16 neurons in each group), the plot is well-fit by a linear regression (r2 = 0.99; Figure 3A; dashed blue line), rather than an exponential curve (r2 = 0.73; Figure 3A; dashed black line).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The slope of the linear regression of ranked ordered mEPSCs is 1.51.
source: We detected a slope of 1.51.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the linear regression analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All measurable excitatory synapses increased by a factor of 1.51 during winter inactivity.
source: The slope of the line from the regression is equal to the scaling factor, implying that all measurable excitatory synapses increased by a factor of 1.51 during winter inactivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the scaling factor derived from the linear regression analysis.

claim: When the winter inactivity mEPSC amplitude distribution is divided by the scaling factor, the 'down-scaled' winter inactivity distribution overlaps the control mEPSC amplitude distribution.
source: Indeed, when the right-shifted cumulative distribution of mEPSC amplitudes from winter inactivity motoneurons (Figure 3B; solid blue line; Kolmogorov-Smirnov test control vs. winter inactivity; p=2.2×10−16) is divided by the scaling factor, the 'down-scaled' winter inactivity distribution (Figure 3B; dashed blue line) overlaps the control mEPSC amplitude distribution (Figure 3B; solid green line; Kolmogorov-Smirnov test control vs. scale winter inactivity; p=0.1403).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Excitatory synapses on inactive respiratory motoneurons 'scale up' during winter inactivity.
source: Therefore, excitatory synapses on inactive respiratory motoneurons 'scale up' during winter inactivity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the linear scaling relationship and overlapping distributions after down-scaling.

claim: Reduced activity may influence the function of intrinsic ion channels to oppose reductions in neuronal and network activity.
source: In addition to synaptic scaling, reduced activity may influence the function of intrinsic ion channels, including Na+, K+, Ca2+, and non-selective cation channels, to oppose reductions in neuronal and network activity.
evidence: This is a general statement about compensatory mechanisms supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Compensatory changes in intrinsic membrane currents during inactivity typically manifest as enhanced excitability in response to injected current.
source: Compensatory changes in the intrinsic membrane currents carried by ion channels during inactivity typically manifest as enhanced excitability in response to injected current (Desai et al., 1999; Echegoyen et al., 2007; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Wilhelm et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Desai et al., 1999; Echegoyen et al., 2007; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Wilhelm et al., 2009.

claim: Firing frequency of respiratory motoneurons did not differ between control and winter inactivity groups at any amount of injected current.
source: We did not observe differences in firing frequency at any amount of current (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The frequency-current (F-I) gain did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons.
source: The frequency-current (F-I) gain did not differ between both groups of motoneurons (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: Resting membrane potential did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons.
source: Additionally, resting membrane potential did not differ between control and winter inactivity motoneurons (control: −57.62 ± 1.74 mV vs. winter inactivity: −57.13 ± 1.41 mV; p=0.8269; T30 = 0.2206).
evidence: This is an experimental finding with statistical analysis.

claim: Respiratory motoneurons do not enhance their excitability in response to winter inactivity.
source: These results suggest that these motoneurons do not enhance their excitability in response to winter inactivity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the lack of changes in firing frequency, F-I gain, and resting membrane potential.

claim: Central pattern generating (CPG) networks in the brainstem underlie the neural activity of respiratory movements in bullfrogs and other vertebrate animals.
source: In bullfrogs and other vertebrate animals, central pattern generating (CPG) networks in the brainstem underlie the neural activity of respiratory movements (Baghdadwala et al., 2015; Feldman et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Baghdadwala et al., 2015 and Feldman et al., 2013.

claim: Respiratory CPG activity is transmitted to cranial and spinal motoneurons, in part, via excitatory glutamatergic synapses.
source: This respiratory CPG activity is transmitted to cranial and spinal motoneurons, in part, via excitatory glutamatergic synapses (Greer et al., 1991; Kottick et al., 2013) to produce the motor output that activates respiratory muscles.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Greer et al., 1991 and Kottick et al., 2013.

claim: In rhythmic respiratory preparations, synaptic properties of motoneurons can be determined by assessing relative changes in the amplitude of the integrated fictive breath after application of receptor antagonists.
source: In rhythmic respiratory preparations, synaptic properties of motoneurons (and premotoneurons) can be determined by assessing relative changes in the amplitude of the integrated fictive breath after application of receptor antagonists, while the activity of the rhythm generating circuits can be assessed through the frequency of fictive breaths (for example Greer et al., 1991; Johnson et al., 2002).
evidence: This methodological approach is supported by citations to Greer et al., 1991 and Johnson et al., 2002.

claim: The activity of the rhythm generating circuits can be assessed through the frequency of fictive breaths.
source: In rhythmic respiratory preparations, synaptic properties of motoneurons (and premotoneurons) can be determined by assessing relative changes in the amplitude of the integrated fictive breath after application of receptor antagonists, while the activity of the rhythm generating circuits can be assessed through the frequency of fictive breaths (for example Greer et al., 1991; Johnson et al., 2002).
evidence: This methodological approach is supported by citations to Greer et al., 1991 and Johnson et al., 2002.

claim: A low concentration of AMPA-receptor antagonist does not influence the amplitude of fictive breaths in control bullfrogs.
source: Using the same in vitro preparation from bullfrogs, Chen and Hedrick (2008) showed that a low concentration of AMPA-receptor antagonist does not influence the amplitude of fictive breaths, while the frequency is more sensitive to inhibition of AMPA-receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen and Hedrick, 2008.

claim: The frequency of fictive breaths is more sensitive to inhibition of AMPA-receptors than amplitude in control bullfrogs.
source: Using the same in vitro preparation from bullfrogs, Chen and Hedrick (2008) showed that a low concentration of AMPA-receptor antagonist does not influence the amplitude of fictive breaths, while the frequency is more sensitive to inhibition of AMPA-receptors.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Chen and Hedrick, 2008.

claim: In control bullfrogs, AMPA-receptor inhibition did not change the amplitude and area of the respiratory-related CN X population discharge.
source: In control bullfrogs, AMPA-receptor inhibition did not change the amplitude and area of the respiratory-related CN X population discharge (Figure 5B,C–D; green traces and bars), corroborating previous results in bullfrogs (Chen and Hedrick, 2008).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B, C-D and corroborated by citation to Chen and Hedrick, 2008.

claim: In bullfrogs following winter inactivity, CN X population output underwent a reduction in amplitude and area during exposure to AMPA-receptor blockade.
source: This was not the case for bullfrogs following winter inactivity. In stark contrast, CN X population output underwent a reduction in amplitude and area during exposure to AMPA-receptor blockade (Figure 5B,C–D, blue traces and bars) and tended to recover toward baseline values following ~1 hr of DNQX washout (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B, C-D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Full transmission of respiratory CPG activity to vagal motoneurons requires an increase in synaptic strength following winter inactivity.
source: These results indicate that full transmission of respiratory CPG activity to vagal motoneurons requires an increase in synaptic strength following winter inactivity.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental finding that AMPA receptor blockade reduces motor output after winter inactivity but not in controls.

claim: Brainstem-spinal cord preparations from winter inactivity bullfrogs produced an elevated number of respiratory bursts at baseline compared to control bullfrogs.
source: With respect to fictive breathing frequency, brainstem-spinal cord preparations from winter inactivity bullfrogs produced an elevated number of respiratory bursts at baseline compared to control bullfrogs (Figure 5B & E2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B and E2.

claim: During exposure to a low concentration of DNQX, both control and winter inactivity bullfrogs decreased fictive-breathing frequency by ~80%.
source: During exposure of the brainstem-spinal cord preparations to a low concentration of DNQX, both control and winter inactivity bullfrogs decreased fictive-breathing frequency by ~80% (Figure 5 E1), suggesting AMPA receptor-sensitive components of the respiratory rhythm generator did not differ.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5E1.

claim: AMPA receptor-sensitive components of the respiratory rhythm generator did not differ between control and winter inactivity bullfrogs.
source: During exposure of the brainstem-spinal cord preparations to a low concentration of DNQX, both control and winter inactivity bullfrogs decreased fictive-breathing frequency by ~80% (Figure 5 E1), suggesting AMPA receptor-sensitive components of the respiratory rhythm generator did not differ.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar response to DNQX in both groups shown in Figure 5E1.

claim: Up-scaling of AMPA-glutamate receptors on vagal motoneurons preserves respiratory motor output after winter inactivity.
source: Collectively, our findings imply that up-scaling of AMPA-glutamate receptors on vagal motoneurons preserves respiratory motor output because, in its absence (i.e., AMPA-receptor inhibition), the amplitude of vagal motoneuron population discharge was approximately 40% less than baseline on average, while respiratory motor amplitude was unaffected by the same concentration of AMPA receptor blocker in control bullfrogs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental findings showing differential effects of AMPA receptor blockade in winter inactivity versus control frogs.

claim: Up-scaling of AMPA receptors in response to inactivity-related stimuli is a physiologically relevant response in an animal normally experiencing extremely low levels of neuronal activity.
source: This result is intriguing because up-scaling commonly occurs in response to experimental decreases in neuronal activity and/or synaptic transmission (Fong et al., 2015; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013; Turrigiano et al., 1998), indicating that up-scaling of AMPA-receptors in response to inactivity-related stimuli is a physiologically relevant response in an animal normally experiencing extremely low levels of neuronal activity.
evidence: This interpretation is supported by citations to previous work and the current experimental findings.

claim: Vagal motoneuron population output driven by respiratory CPG activity was ~40% less than baseline when AMPA receptors were blocked after winter inactivity.
source: Strikingly, we also observed that vagal motoneuron population output driven by respiratory CPG activity was ~40% less than baseline when we, presumably, blocked the effects of scaling with a sub-saturating concentration of AMPA-receptor antagonist after winter inactivity.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from the DNQX experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Amplitude of population motoneuron firing corresponds with drive to respiratory muscles in vivo.
source: Given that amplitude of population motoneuron firing corresponds with drive to respiratory muscles in vivo (Sakakibara, 1984b), up-scaling seems to ensure adequate motor output to critical breathing muscles.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sakakibara, 1984b.

claim: Lung ventilation satisfies gas exchange requirements immediately after winter inactivity in intact, unrestrained bullfrogs.
source: Since lung ventilation satisfies gas exchange requirements immediately after winter inactivity in intact, unrestrained bullfrogs (Santin and Hartzler, 2016a), our findings suggest that scaling of AMPA receptors on respiratory motoneurons may contribute to normal ventilation after months without lung breathing.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Santin and Hartzler, 2016a.

claim: Scaling of AMPA receptors on respiratory motoneurons may contribute to normal ventilation after months without lung breathing.
source: Since lung ventilation satisfies gas exchange requirements immediately after winter inactivity in intact, unrestrained bullfrogs (Santin and Hartzler, 2016a), our findings suggest that scaling of AMPA receptors on respiratory motoneurons may contribute to normal ventilation after months without lung breathing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings and previous work cited.

claim: Increased function of AMPA-glutamate receptors, rather than differences in electrotonic properties, explain the increase in mEPSC amplitude.
source: First, we observed an increase in mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer without changes in neuronal input resistance and mEPSC rise time, indicating that increased function of AMPA-glutamate receptors, rather than differences in electrotonic properties, explain the increase in mEPSC amplitude (Figure 2) (Han and Stevens, 2009).
evidence: This interpretation is supported by the experimental data in Figure 2 and citation to Han and Stevens, 2009.

claim: Ranked ordered mEPSCs from control and winter inactivity distributions were well-fit by a linear regression, a hallmark of synaptic scaling.
source: Second, ranked ordered mEPSCs from control and winter inactivity distributions were well-fit by a linear regression, a hallmark of synaptic scaling, instead of an exponential curve, which describes the rank order relationship following LTP (Figure 3A) (Gainey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3A and citation to Gainey et al., 2009.

claim: Dividing the winter inactivity mEPSC amplitude distribution by the scaling factor produced a 'down-scaled' distribution that overlays the control mEPSC amplitude distribution.
source: Third, dividing the winter inactivity mEPSC amplitude distribution by the scaling factor obtained from the linear fit of ranked order mEPSC amplitudes produced a 'down-scaled' distribution that overlays the control mEPSC amplitude distribution (Figure 3B) (Turrigiano et al., 1998).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data in Figure 3B and citation to Turrigiano et al., 1998.

claim: AMPA-receptors scaled slowly and globally throughout the duration of winter inactivity, rather than rapidly through LTP-like mechanisms.
source: Points two and three imply that AMPA-receptors scaled slowly and globally throughout the duration of winter inactivity, rather than rapidly through LTP-like mechanisms during the time between removal of the frog from the simulated winter environment and ~3 hr later when the recordings were made.
evidence: This is inferred from the linear scaling relationship and overlapping distributions after down-scaling.

claim: Increased synaptic strength enhanced the contribution of AMPA-receptors for producing respiratory motoneuron discharge.
source: Finally, increased synaptic strength enhanced the contribution of AMPA-receptors for producing respiratory motoneuron discharge.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the experimental findings from the DNQX experiments in Figure 5.

claim: Vagal motoneurons receiving respiratory CPG input reduced motoneuron population amplitude by ~40% after winter inactivity upon exposure to a low concentration of AMPA-receptor antagonist.
source: Unlike control bullfrogs, vagal motoneurons receiving respiratory CPG input reduced motoneuron population amplitude by ~40% after winter inactivity upon exposure to a low concentration of AMPA-receptor antagonist (Figure 5).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Respiratory output leaving the brainstem through the vagus nerve would have been absolutely smaller in bullfrogs after winter inactivity if scaling did not occur.
source: Consistent with a compensatory or homeostatic response, this result suggests that respiratory output leaving the brainstem through the vagus nerve would have been absolutely smaller in bullfrogs after winter inactivity if scaling did not occur.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental finding that AMPA receptor blockade reduces motor output after winter inactivity.

claim: Motoneuron population discharge increases proportionally with outflow to respiratory muscles in vivo.
source: Since motoneuron population discharge increases proportionally with outflow to respiratory muscles in vivo (Sakakibara, 1984b), we collectively interpret our results to mean that scaling of AMPA-receptors on respiratory motoneurons is part of a strategy used to preserve respiratory motor output that produces appropriate lung breathing after winter inactivity.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sakakibara, 1984b.

claim: Scaling of AMPA-receptors on respiratory motoneurons is part of a strategy used to preserve respiratory motor output that produces appropriate lung breathing after winter inactivity.
source: Since motoneuron population discharge increases proportionally with outflow to respiratory muscles in vivo (Sakakibara, 1984b), we collectively interpret our results to mean that scaling of AMPA-receptors on respiratory motoneurons is part of a strategy used to preserve respiratory motor output that produces appropriate lung breathing after winter inactivity.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study based on all the experimental findings and cited literature.

claim: Upregulation of AMPA-receptors probably does not underlie the facilitation of fictive-breathing frequency following winter inactivity.
source: Although the amplitude of vagal motoneuron output became increasingly reliant on AMPA-receptors following winter inactivity, upregulation of AMPA-receptors probably does not underlie the facilitation of fictive-breathing frequency that we observed (Figure 5E present study, Santin and Hartzler, 2016b).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5E and citation to Santin and Hartzler, 2016b.

claim: Respiratory rhythm generating circuits use distinct mechanisms of compensation to enhance the frequency of respiratory-related discharge following winter inactivity.
source: This implies that respiratory rhythm generating circuits use distinct mechanisms of compensation to enhance the frequency of respiratory-related discharge following winter inactivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that frequency and amplitude are differentially affected by winter inactivity.

claim: The glottal dilator muscle gates airflow into and out of the lungs during ventilation in anuran amphibians.
source: The glottal dilator muscle gates airflow into and out of the lungs during ventilation in anuran amphibians (Gans et al., 1969) and receives its innervation from the laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve that arises the fourth rootlet of the IX-X complex in anurans (Stuesse et al., 1984; Yamaguchi et al., 2003; Zornik and Kelley, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gans et al., 1969; Stuesse et al., 1984; Yamaguchi et al., 2003; Zornik and Kelley, 2007.

claim: The glottal dilator receives its innervation from the laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve that arises from the fourth rootlet of the IX-X complex in anurans.
source: The glottal dilator muscle gates airflow into and out of the lungs during ventilation in anuran amphibians (Gans et al., 1969) and receives its innervation from the laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve that arises the fourth rootlet of the IX-X complex in anurans (Stuesse et al., 1984; Yamaguchi et al., 2003; Zornik and Kelley, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stuesse et al., 1984; Yamaguchi et al., 2003; Zornik and Kelley, 2007.

claim: The fourth root of the IX-X nerve is composed of axons mostly projecting to laryngeal muscles.
source: The fourth root of the IX-X nerve is composed of axons mostly projecting to laryngeal muscles (Simpson et al., 1986).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Simpson et al., 1986.

claim: Laryngeal motoneurons are morphologically distinct from gastric and cardiac vagal motoneurons with double the soma diameter of the long axis.
source: Furthermore, laryngeal motoneurons are morphologically distinct from gastric and cardiac vagal motoneurons (double the soma diameter of the long axis) that reside in the same area (Matesz and Székely, 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Matesz and Székely, 1996.

claim: All mEPSCs recorded at −80 mV were blocked by DNQX.
source: All mEPSCs that we could detect were blocked by DNQX.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from the voltage clamp experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Winter inactivity resulted in elevated mEPSC amplitude.
source: Winter inactivity resulted in elevated mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer, but not frequency.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Winter inactivity resulted in elevated mEPSC charge transfer.
source: Winter inactivity resulted in elevated mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer, but not frequency.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Winter inactivity did not result in elevated mEPSC frequency.
source: Winter inactivity resulted in elevated mEPSC amplitude and charge transfer, but not frequency.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Control and winter inactivity mEPSC amplitude distributions are significantly different (p<2.2×10−16).
source: Kolomogorov-Smirnov tests revealed that control and winter inactivity are significantly different (p<2.2×10−16), but control and scaled winter-inactivity distributions were not significantly different (p=0.1403).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Control and scaled winter-inactivity mEPSC amplitude distributions were not significantly different (p=0.1403).
source: Kolomogorov-Smirnov tests revealed that control and winter inactivity are significantly different (p<2.2×10−16), but control and scaled winter-inactivity distributions were not significantly different (p=0.1403).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was no difference in the slope of mean firing frequency-current relationship between control and winter inactivity motoneurons (p=0.9147).
source: There was no difference in in the slope of mean firing frequency-current relationship (p=0.9147; Analysis of Covariance).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the Analysis of Covariance shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In winter inactivity bullfrogs, DNQX led to a significant decrease in burst amplitude compared to control bullfrogs.
source: In winter inactivity bullfrogs, DNQX led to a significant decrease in burst amplitude and area compared to control bullfrogs.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5C1.

claim: In winter inactivity bullfrogs, DNQX led to a significant decrease in burst area compared to control bullfrogs.
source: In winter inactivity bullfrogs, DNQX led to a significant decrease in burst amplitude and area compared to control bullfrogs.
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5D1.

claim: DNQX caused a decrease in fictive lung burst frequency in both groups of frogs.
source: DNQX caused a decrease in fictive lung burst frequency in both groups of frogs despite winter inactivity frogs starting from a higher baseline (Figure 5E2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5E2.

claim: Winter inactivity frogs had a higher baseline fictive lung burst frequency than control frogs.
source: DNQX caused a decrease in fictive lung burst frequency in both groups of frogs despite winter inactivity frogs starting from a higher baseline (Figure 5E2).
evidence: This is an experimental finding supported by data shown in Figure 5E2.

claim: Burst amplitudes from control frogs do not differ between DNQX and washout (p=0.3113).
source: Burst amplitudes from control frogs do not differ between DNQX and washout (B. DNQX vs. washout; p=0.3113) and were not different than 100% of baseline during DNQX or washout (one sample t test; p=0.7998 during DNQX and p=0.3808 during washout, n = 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the washout experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Burst amplitudes from control frogs were not different than 100% of baseline during DNQX (p=0.7998).
source: Burst amplitudes from control frogs do not differ between DNQX and washout (B. DNQX vs. washout; p=0.3113) and were not different than 100% of baseline during DNQX or washout (one sample t test; p=0.7998 during DNQX and p=0.3808 during washout, n = 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the washout experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Burst amplitudes from control frogs were not different than 100% of baseline during washout (p=0.3808).
source: Burst amplitudes from control frogs do not differ between DNQX and washout (B. DNQX vs. washout; p=0.3113) and were not different than 100% of baseline during DNQX or washout (one sample t test; p=0.7998 during DNQX and p=0.3808 during washout, n = 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the washout experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Experiments were approved by the Wright State University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol number 1047).
source: Experiments were approved by the Wright State University Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocol number 1047).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval for the experiments.

claim: Control bullfrogs were maintained at 22°C.
source: Two groups of adult, female bullfrogs, Lithobates catesbeianus, were used in this study: (1) control frogs maintained at 22°C (n = 13) and (2) frogs experiencing an overwintering-like environment (n = 11).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the control group.

claim: Winter inactivity frogs experienced an overwintering-like environment.
source: Two groups of adult, female bullfrogs, Lithobates catesbeianus, were used in this study: (1) control frogs maintained at 22°C (n = 13) and (2) frogs experiencing an overwintering-like environment (n = 11).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for the winter inactivity group.

claim: Water temperature was gradually cooled to 2°C over 6 weeks for winter inactivity frogs.
source: Winter inactivity frogs were kept in a plastic tank under the same conditions as control frogs for ~1 week before water temperature was gradually cooled to 2°C over 6 weeks (~3.3°C decrease per week) in a walk-in, temperature-controlled environmental chamber.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for creating the winter inactivity condition.

claim: After 8 weeks of submergence, experiments commenced for winter inactivity frogs.
source: Once water temperature reached 2°C, air access was denied using a plastic screen placed in the tank. After 8 weeks of submergence, experiments commenced.
evidence: This describes the timing of experiments for the winter inactivity group.

claim: The brainstem-spinal cord was dissected in bullfrog artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF).
source: The dissection was performed in bullfrog artificial cerebrospinal fluid (aCSF; concentrations in mM: 104 NaCl, 4 KCl, 1.4 MgCl2, 7.5 glucose, 40 NaHCO3, 2.5 CaCl2 and 1 NaH2PO4, and gassed with 90% O2, 1.3%CO2, balance N2; pH = 7.8; CO2/pH values reflect normal for bullfrogs).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for tissue preparation.

claim: Three hours was sufficient to label motoneurons with tetramethylrhodamine-dextran.
source: The dye was allowed to diffuse for 3 hr while the brain was superfused with gassed aCSF at 10 mL min−1. We found that 3 hr was sufficient to label motoneurons (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation about the labeling protocol shown in Figure 1.

claim: Brainstem slices were 300-μM-thick.
source: Following the 3 hr incubation period, we glued the brainstem to an agar block and then cut 300-μM-thick brainstem slices using a Vibratome tissue slicer (Leica Microsystems, Buffalo Grove, IL) in cold, gassed aCSF as previously described (Santin and Hartzler, 2016b).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for slice preparation.

claim: Brainstem slices within 600 μm rostral to the obex were used to maximize the likelihood of recording from laryngeal motoneurons that innervate the glottal dilator muscle.
source: To maximize the likelihood that we recorded from laryngeal motoneurons that innervate the glottal dilator muscle, we (1) used brainstem slices within 600 μm rostral to the obex (Stuesse et al., 1984) and (2) selected labeled neurons with a long soma diameter >20 μm as these neurons are not visceral motoneurons (Matesz and Székely, 1996).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for selecting appropriate slices, supported by citations to Stuesse et al., 1984 and Matesz and Székely, 1996.

claim: Labeled neurons with a long soma diameter >20 μm were selected as these neurons are not visceral motoneurons.
source: To maximize the likelihood that we recorded from laryngeal motoneurons that innervate the glottal dilator muscle, we (1) used brainstem slices within 600 μm rostral to the obex (Stuesse et al., 1984) and (2) selected labeled neurons with a long soma diameter >20 μm as these neurons are not visceral motoneurons (Matesz and Székely, 1996).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for selecting appropriate neurons, supported by citation to Matesz and Székely, 1996.

claim: Borosilicate glass pipettes had a resistance of 2–4 MΩ.
source: Borosilicate glass pipettes were back-filled with intracellular solution containing (in mM): 110 potassium gluconate, 2 MgCl2, 10 Hepes, 1 Na2 -ATP, 0.1 Na2-GTP, 2.5 EGTA, pH 7.2 with KOH, and positioned over an AgCl2-coated Ag wire with a resistance of 2–4 MΩ.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for patch clamp recordings.

claim: Data were low-pass filtered at 2 kHz and acquired at 10 kHz for current clamp experiments.
source: Data were low-pass filtered at 2 kHz and acquired at 10 kHz for current clamp experiments and 100 kHz for voltage-clamp experiments with an Axopatch 200B amplifier, Digidata 1440A A/D converter, and Molecular Devices P10 Clampex software (Molecular Devices, Sunnydale, CA).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for data acquisition.

claim: Data were acquired at 100 kHz for voltage-clamp experiments.
source: Data were low-pass filtered at 2 kHz and acquired at 10 kHz for current clamp experiments and 100 kHz for voltage-clamp experiments with an Axopatch 200B amplifier, Digidata 1440A A/D converter, and Molecular Devices P10 Clampex software (Molecular Devices, Sunnydale, CA).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for data acquisition.

claim: All voltages from voltage- and current-clamp experiments were corrected for a liquid junction potential of −12 mV.
source: All voltages from voltage- and current-clamp experiments were corrected for a liquid junction potential of −12 mV (pipette relative to the bath).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for voltage correction.

claim: Neurons with membrane voltages more negative than −45 mV and that contained >50 mV action potentials were used in analysis.
source: Neurons with membrane voltages more negative than −45 mV and that contained >50 mV action potentials were used in analysis.
evidence: This describes the inclusion criteria for neurons in the analysis.

claim: Series resistance (Rs) was not compensated in voltage clamp experiments.
source: Rs was not compensated, but if Rs changed by >20% during the recording or was large (>25 MΩ), the neuron was discarded from analysis.
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for voltage clamp recordings.

claim: If series resistance changed by >20% during the recording or was large (>25 MΩ), the neuron was discarded from analysis.
source: Rs was not compensated, but if Rs changed by >20% during the recording or was large (>25 MΩ), the neuron was discarded from analysis.
evidence: This describes the exclusion criteria for neurons in the analysis.

claim: 500 nM tetrodotoxin (TTX) was bath applied for 5 min to block voltage-gated Na+ channels.
source: 500 nM tetrodotoxin (TTX) was bath applied for 5 min to block voltage-gated Na+ channels, and then 1 min of mEPSCs were recorded.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for recording mEPSCs.

claim: All mEPSCs from both groups of frogs recorded at −80 mV were blocked by 10 μM DNQX.
source: Next, the neuron was superfused with 10 μM DNQX +500 nM TTX to confirm the AMPA-ergic identity of the mEPSCs. All mEPSCs from both groups of frogs recorded at – 80 mV were blocked by 10 μM DNQX.
evidence: This is an experimental observation confirming the identity of the mEPSCs.

claim: Spinal nerve II (SN II) is the hypoglossal nerve in anuran amphibians.
source: Spinal nerve II (SN II; the hypoglossal nerve in anuran amphibians) and cranial nerve X (CN X; vagus) contain branches that innervate the respiratory muscles of amphibians; therefore, spontaneous, rhythmic activity recorded through these cranial nerves corresponds with respiratory rhythm/pattern generator central nervous system activity that drives breathing in intact frogs (Sakakibara, 1984a).
evidence: This is a statement about amphibian anatomy supported by citation to Sakakibara, 1984a.

claim: Spontaneous, rhythmic activity recorded through SN II and CN X corresponds with respiratory rhythm/pattern generator central nervous system activity that drives breathing in intact frogs.
source: Spinal nerve II (SN II; the hypoglossal nerve in anuran amphibians) and cranial nerve X (CN X; vagus) contain branches that innervate the respiratory muscles of amphibians; therefore, spontaneous, rhythmic activity recorded through these cranial nerves corresponds with respiratory rhythm/pattern generator central nervous system activity that drives breathing in intact frogs (Sakakibara, 1984a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sakakibara, 1984a.

claim: Nerve activity was amplified ×1000 using differential amplifiers.
source: Nerve activity was amplified ×1000 using differential amplifiers (DP-311; Warner Instruments, Hamden, CT), filtered (100–1000 Hz), full-wave rectified, integrated (time constant, 60 ms) and recorded using the Powerlab 8/35 data acquisition system (ADInstruments Inc., Colorado Springs, CO).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods for recording nerve activity.

claim: The preparation was allowed 1 hr to stabilize following dissection before recording baseline respiratory bursting.
source: The preparation was allowed 1 hr to stabilize following dissection and then recording of baseline respiratory bursting in gassed aCSF occurred for 20–30 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for extracellular recordings.

claim: The preparation was exposed to 4 μM DNQX for 40 min.
source: After this baseline period, the preparation was exposed to 4 μM DNQX for 40 min.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol for DNQX application.

claim: Events below 7.5 pA were rejected in mEPSC analysis, as this value is about double the background noise.
source: We rejected events below 7.5 pA, as this value is about double the background noise and detection was unreliable.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for mEPSCs.

claim: The first 50 mEPSCs from each neuron were used for rank ordering mEPSC amplitudes and construction of cumulative probability histogram.
source: For rank ordering mEPSC amplitudes and construction of cumulative probability histogram (Figure 3), we used the first 50 mEPSCs from the minute of data obtained from each neuron.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for Figure 3.

claim: The amplitude average of the first 50 mEPSCs for each neuron was within ~1–2 pA of the average obtained using 1 min of data.
source: The amplitude average of the first 50 mEPSCs for each neuron was within ~1–2 pA of the average obtained using 1 mine of data.
evidence: This is an observation about the consistency of the sampling method.

claim: Scaled mEPSCs below 7.5 pA were not included in analysis because mEPSC amplitudes below this value are not represented in the control distribution.
source: We only included scaled values that were above the noise threshold of 7.5 pA, as mEPSC amplitudes below this value are not represented in the control distribution and would produce erroneous results in statistical analysis (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for scaled mEPSCs, supported by citation to Kim et al., 2012.

claim: Input resistance was calculated as slope of the voltage-current relationship in response to negative current injections.
source: For current-clamp experiments, input resistance was calculated as slope of the voltage-current relationship in response to negative current injections (−150 pA to 0 pA in 50 pA steps, 0.5 s steps).
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for input resistance.

claim: Activity on the vagus nerve was classified as a respiratory burst if it occurred near-synchronously with the hypoglossal and if they were ~1 s in duration.
source: For extracellular nerve recordings from the in vitro brainstem-spinal cord preparation, activity on the vagus nerve was classified as a respiratory burst if it occurred near-synchronously with the hypoglossal and if they were ~1 s in duration.
evidence: This describes the criteria for identifying respiratory bursts in the data analysis.

claim: Ten minutes of burst data were analyzed in control before application of 4 μM DNQX.
source: We analyzed 10 min of burst data in control before application of 4 μM DNQX, the last 10 min of burst data after 40 min of exposure to 4 μM DNQX, and 10 min of data ~ 1 hr after washing DNQX.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for extracellular recordings.

claim: The last 10 min of burst data after 40 min of exposure to 4 μM DNQX were analyzed.
source: We analyzed 10 min of burst data in control before application of 4 μM DNQX, the last 10 min of burst data after 40 min of exposure to 4 μM DNQX, and 10 min of data ~ 1 hr after washing DNQX.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for extracellular recordings.

claim: Ten minutes of data approximately 1 hr after washing DNQX were analyzed.
source: We analyzed 10 min of burst data in control before application of 4 μM DNQX, the last 10 min of burst data after 40 min of exposure to 4 μM DNQX, and 10 min of data ~ 1 hr after washing DNQX.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for extracellular recordings.

claim: Fictive-breath amplitude was analyzed as the maximum height subtracted from the baseline at the start of each burst of the integrated neurogram.
source: Fictive-breath amplitude was analyzed as the maximum height subtracted from the baseline at the start of each burst of the integrated neurogram.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for fictive-breath amplitude.

claim: Fictive-breath area was obtained from the area under the curve of the integrated nerve burst.
source: Fictive-breath area was obtained from the area under the curve of the integrated nerve burst.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for fictive-breath area.

claim: Fictive-breath properties in DNQX and washout are expressed as a percent change from baseline or a percent of baseline.
source: Fictive-breath properties in DNQX and washout are expressed as a percent change from baseline or a percent of baseline.
evidence: This describes the data analysis methods for expressing fictive-breath properties.

claim: The number of neurons (n = 16 per group) and/or animals (nine control frogs and seven winter inactivity frogs) studied in synaptic and firing frequency experiments are consistent with other studies determining compensatory changes in neurophysiological properties in response to activity perturbations.
source: The number of neurons (n = 16 per group) and/or animals (nine control frogs and seven winter inactivity frogs) studied in synaptic and firing frequency experiments are consistent with other studies determining compensatory changes in neurophysiological properties in response to activity perturbations (e.g. Wilhelm et al., 2009; Knogler et al., 2010; Lambo and Turrigiano, 2013).
evidence: This justifies the sample size used in the study by citing similar studies.

claim: Four brainstems per group were used for in vitro brainstem experiments of rhythmic respiratory activity in response to AMPA-receptor inhibition.
source: For in vitro brainstem experiments of rhythmic respiratory activity in response to AMPA-receptor inhibition, four brainstems per group were used.
evidence: This describes the sample size for the extracellular recording experiments.

claim: Statistical significance was accepted when p<0.05.
source: Statistical significance was accepted when p<0.05.
evidence: This describes the statistical threshold used in the study.
